short: Introduced in 215 CE as a double-value silver coin, the antoninianus was debased within decades and abandoned by Diocletian's reform.
full:
In early 215, Caracalla introduced the antoninianus, a coin distinguished by the emperor's radiate crown and valued at two denarii despite weighing only about 1.6 times as much silver, an immediate, if modest, debasement dressed as a new denomination. It gradually displaced the denarius as the empire's principal silver coin over the following decades.

Successive emperors debased it further to cover military spending; by Gallienus's reign in the 260s it carried under five percent silver, little more than coated bronze. Aurelian's reform of 274 restored some silver and marked coins with a fixed ratio to rebuild trust, but the denomination was ultimately abandoned in Diocletian's currency reform of 294, replaced by a new system of gold, silver and bronze coins bearing no relation to the old debased currency.
